title: Carnot Engine and Reversible Thermodynamic Cycles
short_intro: A Carnot engine is an idealized thermal engine operating on a reversible thermodynamic cycle consisting of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes. It establishes the theoretical upper limit for the conversion of heat into mechanical work between two thermal reservoirs.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of efficiency, dependence on source and sink temperatures, calculation of work done, and direct application of Carnot efficiency formula.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Coefficient of performance of refrigerators, Carnot theorem proofs, entropy changes in reversible and irreversible cycles, and T-S diagram analysis.

prerequisites: First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics

concept_notes.heading: Cycle Structure and Processes
bullets: The Carnot cycle comprises four successive reversible processes: isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, and adiabatic compression.
During isothermal stages, the working substance is in thermal contact with a heat reservoir maintaining constant temperature T<sub>1</sub> or T<sub>2</sub>.
During adiabatic stages, the system is thermally isolated, and temperature changes from T<sub>1<sup>&#9circ;</sup></sub> to T<sub>2</sub> without heat exchange.

concept_notes.heading: Efficiency of a Carnot Engine
bullets: Efficiency (&eta;) is defined as the ratio of net mechanical work done by the engine to the total heat absorbed from the high-temperature source.
It depends exclusively on the absolute temperatures of the source (T<sub>1</sub>) and the sink (T<sub>2</sub>), expressed as &eta; = 1 - (T<sub>2</sub> / T<sub>1</sub>).
Efficiency is always less than unity unless the sink temperature T<sub>2</sub> is absolute zero, which is unattainable by the Third Law of Thermodynamics.

concept_notes.heading: Carnot's Theorem
bullets: No heat engine operating between two given thermal reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible Carnot engine operating between the same two reservoirs.
All reversible engines operating between the same two temperatures have the same efficiency, regardless of the working substance used.
The theorem provides the fundamental basis for defining the thermodynamic absolute temperature scale.

concept_notes.heading: Carnot Refrigerator and Heat Pump
bullets: Running a Carnot cycle in reverse converts it into a refrigerator or heat pump, transferring heat from a low-temperature sink to a high-temperature source by consuming external work.
The coefficient of performance (COP) for a refrigerator is given by COP<sub>ref</sub> = T<sub>2</sub> / (T<sub>1</sub> - T<sub>2</sub>).
For a heat pump, COP<sub>hp</sub> = T<sub>1</sub> / (T<sub>1</sub> - T<sub>2</sub>) = COP<sub>ref</sub> + 1.

derivations.title: Derivation of Carnot Engine Efficiency
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas working substance operating in a complete cyclic process.
steps: Step 1: Write heat absorbed during isothermal expansion at temperature T<sub>1</sub> from volume V<sub>1</sub> to V<sub>2</sub>: Q<sub>1</sub> = nRT<sub>1</sub> ln(V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>).
Step 2: Write heat rejected during isothermal compression at temperature T<sub>2</sub> from volume V<sub>4</sub> to V<sub>3</sub>: Q<sub>2</sub> = nRT<sub>2</sub> ln(V<sub>3</sub>/V<sub>4</sub>).

Step 3: Relate volumes during intermediate adiabatic processes: T<sub>1</sub>V<sub>2</sub><sup>&gamma;-1</sup> = T<sub>2</sub>V<sub>3</sub><sup>&gamma;-1</sup> and T<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub><sup>&gamma;-1</sup> = T<sub>2</sub>V<sub>4</sub><sup>&gamma;-1</sup>, yielding V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>3</sub>/V<sub>4</sub>.
Step 4: Substitute heat values into efficiency definition &eta; = 1 - (Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>).

derivations.title: Coefficient of Performance of a Carnot Refrigerator
derivations.conditions: Reversed Carnot cycle operating between temperatures T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>.
steps: Step 1: Define COP as desired output over required input: COP = Q<sub>2</sub> / W.
Step 2: Apply conservation of energy to the cycle: W = Q<sub>1</sub> - Q<sub>2</sub>.

Step 3: Substitute Q<sub>1</sub>/Q<sub>2</sub> = T<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>2</sub> into the COP expression: COP = Q<sub>2</sub> / (Q<sub>1</sub> - Q<sub>2</sub>) = (Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>) / (1 - Q<sub>2</sub>/Q<sub>1</sub>).
Step 4: Replace heat ratio with absolute temperature ratio.

graphs_and_experiments.title: P-V Diagram of Carnot Cycle
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A closed loop on a pressure-volume plane consisting of two hyperbolic isothermal curves (T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>) connected by two steeper adiabatic curves.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area enclosed by the cycle represents the net mechanical work done by the engine during one complete cycle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in identifying cycle directions, calculating work via area integration, and distinguishing isothermal from adiabatic slopes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: T-S (Temperature-Entropy) Diagram of Carnot Cycle
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangle on the temperature-entropy plane bounded by temperatures T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub> and entropy values S<sub>A</sub> and S<sub>B</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area of the rectangle represents the total heat absorbed (Q<sub>1</sub>), and the lower inner area represents heat rejected (Q<sub>2</sub>). The difference represents net work.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in advanced PGT questions to evaluate entropy transformations and simplify graphical efficiency calculations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Efficiency vs Sink Temperature Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A downward sloping curve (or straight line depending on variable representation) showing &eta; decreasing as T<sub>2</sub> increases for a fixed T<sub>1</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that efficiency increases as the temperature difference (T<sub>1</sub> - T<sub>2</sub>) increases.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding thermal plant optimization and limits of efficiency.

solved_numericals.question: A Carnot engine operates between a source at 500 K and a sink at 300 K. If it absorbs 1200 J of heat from the source, calculate the work done by the engine.
solution_steps: Step 1: Identify given parameters: T<sub>1</sub> = 500 K, T<sub>2</sub> = 300 K, Q<sub>1</sub> = 1200 J.
Step 3: Calculate work done using W = &eta; * Q<sub>1</sub> = 0.4 * 1200 J = 480 J.

solved_numericals.question: A Carnot refrigerator absorbs heat from a freezer maintained at -23°C and rejects heat to the surrounding room at 27°C. If 500 J of work is consumed per cycle, find the heat rejected to the room.
solution_steps: Step 1: Convert temperatures to Kelvin: T<sub>2</sub> = -23 + 273 = 250 K, T<sub>1</sub> = 27 + 273 = 300 K.
Step 2: Calculate COP of the refrigerator using COP = T<sub>2</sub> / (T<sub>1</sub> - T<sub>2</sub>) = 250 / (300 - 250) = 250 / 50 = 5.
Step 3: Relate COP to heat removed: COP = Q<sub>2</sub> / W &rArr; Q<sub>2</sub> = COP * W = 5 * 500 J = 2500 J.
Step 4: Calculate heat rejected Q<sub>1</sub> = Q<sub>2</sub> + W = 2500 J + 500 J = 3000 J.

solved_numericals.question: By what percentage does the efficiency of a Carnot engine increase if the source temperature is raised from 500 K to 600 K, while the sink temperature remains constant at 300 K?
solution_steps: Step 3: Calculate percentage increase in efficiency: ((&eta;<sub>f</sub> - &eta;<sub>i</sub>) / &eta;<sub>i</sub>) * 100 = ((0.5 - 0.4) / 0.4) * 100 = (0.1 / 0.4) * 100 = 25%.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Working parts are frictionless and thermal insulation is perfect, which is practically impossible to achieve in real engineering systems.
Limitation: The Carnot cycle is quasistatic and infinitely slow, rendering it useless for practical high-power output engines operating at finite speeds.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A Carnot engine can achieve 100% efficiency if the sink is kept at room temperature.
common_misconceptions.correct: 100% efficiency is impossible unless the sink is at absolute zero (0 K), which violates the Third Law of Thermodynamics.
common_misconceptions.why: Efficiency depends on the ratio T<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>1</sub>; as long as T<sub>2</sub> is above zero, some heat must be rejected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends on the nature of the working fluid (e.g., whether it is a monoatomic or diatomic gas).
common_misconceptions.correct: The efficiency depends solely on the temperatures of the source and sink.
common_misconceptions.why: Carnot's theorem proves that efficiency is independent of the working substance.

quick_revision: Carnot efficiency depends only on source and sink absolute temperatures: &eta; = 1 - (T<sub>2</sub> / T<sub>1</sub>).
Work Done in Carnot Cycle: W = Q_1 - Q_2 = nR(T_1 - T_2)\ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)
